# Introduction

Handwriting is personal, and examiners have long used it to judge who wrote a document. Reviews of writer identification describe how the field moved from hand-made features to machine learning and, more recently, deep learning [@rehman2019]. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) learn features straight from the pixels and have been used to identify writers from images of their handwriting [@he2019; @gu2018]. A second route treats the problem as similarity learning: instead of naming the writer, a Siamese network judges whether two samples came from the same hand, so it can be applied to writers it has not seen [@chicco2021]. This report builds both models on simulated images of the digits 0 to 4 written by 20 writers. We explore the data (Task 1), fit a CNN that identifies the writer (Task 2), fit a Siamese network that verifies whether two images share a writer (Task 3), explain how the data were split and how leakage was avoided (Task 4), tune the CNN (Task 5) and compare the two models (Task 6).

# Data exploration {#sec-task1}

```{r}
#| label: task1-load
#| include: false
##Task 1: Exploration of the data

data <- readRDS(data_path)
dim(data$images)
head(data$metadata)
metadata <- data$metadata

#This gets the data ready for the neural network
x <- data$images / 255 #makes copy of images with every pixel divided by 255 so
#values run from 0 to 1. Neural networks learn better with smaller numbers
#takes writer ids and makes it 0 to 19 instead of 1 to 20, keras start counting from 0
y_person <- data$metadata$person_id - 1L
#x is what the model looks at (images) then y is the person (or our answer that we are trying to predict.)


table(metadata$person_id, metadata$session) #250 images per person per session

dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)

# Draw one image from its row number
draw_image <- function(i){
  m <- x[i, , , 1]
  image(t(m[28:1, ]), col = gray.colors(256, start = 1, end = 0),
        axes = FALSE, asp = 1)
}

# All 20 writers for one digit (session and replicate fixed)
plot_writers <- function(d, s = 1, r = 1){
  op <- par(mfrow = c(4, 5), mar = c(0.3, 0.3, 1.5, 0.3), oma = c(0, 0, 2.5, 0))
  on.exit(par(op))
  for (p in 1:20){
    i <- which(metadata$person_id == p & metadata$digit == d &
                 metadata$session == s & metadata$replicate == r)
    draw_image(i)
    title(paste("Writer", p), cex.main = 0.9)
  }
  mtext(paste0("Digit ", d, " (session ", s, ", replicate ", r, ")"),
        outer = TRUE, font = 2)
}

# Random sample of writers across sessions (replicate fixed)
plot_sessions_sample <- function(d, n_people = 10, r = 1, seed = 1){
  set.seed(seed)
  people <- sort(sample(1:20, n_people))
  op <- par(mfrow = c(n_people, 5), mar = c(0.2, 0.2, 1.2, 0.2),
            oma = c(0, 5, 2.5, 0), xpd = NA)
  on.exit(par(op))
  for (p in people){
    for (s in 1:5){
      i <- which(metadata$person_id == p & metadata$digit == d &
                   metadata$session == s & metadata$replicate == r)
      draw_image(i)
      if (p == people[1]) title(paste("Session", s), cex.main = 0.9)
      if (s == 1) mtext(paste("Writer", p), side = 2, line = 0.5, las = 1, cex = 0.7)
    }
  }
  mtext(paste0("Digit ", d, " across sessions (replicate ", r, ")"),
        outer = TRUE, font = 2)
}

# Same writers across replicates (session fixed)
plot_replicates <- function(d, s = 1, n_people = 10,
                            reps = c(1, 11, 21, 31, 41), seed = 1){
  set.seed(seed)
  people <- sort(sample(1:20, n_people))
  op <- par(mfrow = c(n_people, length(reps)), mar = c(0.2, 0.2, 1.2, 0.2),
            oma = c(0, 5, 2.5, 0), xpd = NA)
  on.exit(par(op))
  for (p in people){
    for (r in reps){
      i <- which(metadata$person_id == p & metadata$digit == d &
                   metadata$session == s & metadata$replicate == r)
      draw_image(i)
      if (p == people[1]) title(paste("Replicate", r), cex.main = 0.9)
      if (r == reps[1]) mtext(paste("Writer", p), side = 2, line = 0.5, las = 1, cex = 0.7)
    }
  }
  mtext(paste0("Digit ", d, " across replicates (session ", s, ")"),
        outer = TRUE, font = 2)
}
```

## Data Overview

The data consisted of 25,000 greyscale images of 28 x 28 pixels, showing the digits 0 to 4. Each of the 20 writers wrote each digit 50 times (replicate) in each of the 5 sessions, giving a total of 1,250 images per writer. The original pixel values \[0,255\], were scaled to \[0, 1\] before fitting the neural network models, because inputs on a small common scale make gradient-based training more stable [@goodfellow2016; @chollet2022]. The metadata contains the image ID, writer ID, digit, session number and replicate number. To explore the sources of variability in the data, four analyses were carried out including variation between writers, variation across sessions for a subset of writers, variation within sessions (across replicates) for a subset of writers, and a quantitative comparison of the three using pixel distances.

## Variation between writers

To examine variation between writers, each digit was plotted for all 20 writers, with session and replicate fixed at 1. This produced five plots, one per digit. Writer-identification methods rely on the fact that people differ in features such as size, shape and slant [@rehman2019], so we looked for these features. @fig-writers shows clear differences in handwriting style between the 20 writers.

```{r}
#| label: fig-writers
#| fig-cap: "Digits 0 and 1 for all 20 writers, with session 1 and replicate 1 fixed."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "Digit 0"
#|   - "Digit 1"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5
plot_writers(0)
plot_writers(1)
```

Variation in shape is most clearly observed in digits 0 and 1 (@fig-writers). For example, although all the 1s have a base, some have a hook at the top (writers 1, 7 and 14), while others have a curved body that resembles the digit 2 (writers 3, 9 and 17). For digit 0, shapes vary from round to oval, and some writers (10, 12, 13 and 19) draw squarer shapes with a flat top. The remaining digits follow a more consistent style, with the primary differences being slant and size. Size also varies whereby some writers (3 and 9) write small and compact digits, while others fill the space with large digits. Slant varies from upright to a rightward slant (writers 18 and 10), while writer 19 slants to the left. These differences in size, shape and slant are features that the models could learn. The plots for digits 2, 3 and 4 are in @fig-app-writers (Appendix A).

## Variation across sessions

To assess whether a person's handwriting changes between sessions, 10 writers were randomly sampled and each digit was plotted across the 5 sessions, with the replicate fixed at 1. The plots for digits 2, 3 and 4 are in @fig-app-sessions (Appendix A).

```{r}
#| label: fig-sessions
#| fig-cap: "Digits 1 and 0 for ten randomly sampled writers (seed 1), with replicate 1 fixed. Rows are writers and columns are sessions 1 to 5."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "Digit 1"
#|   - "Digit 0"
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 10
plot_sessions_sample(1)
plot_sessions_sample(0)
```

There are visible changes in style between sessions, and these are more noticeable for some writers than for others. Although some changes are noticeable, some writers remained consistent in certain characteristics. For example, writer 3 wrote small digits in all sessions and, for digit 1, kept their signature hook in every session, as writer 17 did. Other writers changed their characteristic style, for example, writer 19 slanted the digits slightly to the left in the first session, but the digits became more upright as the sessions progressed. Writer 1's 1s also changed between sessions because some have hooks and the lengths of the strokes differ. This indicates that a writer's handwriting may change between sessions. Although some of these changes are minor, they alter a writer's characteristic style from session 1, so the models may identify some writers less accurately in a new session.

## Variation across replicates

```{r}
#| label: fig-replicates
#| fig-cap: "Digit 1 for the same ten writers as in the sessions figure, with session 1 fixed and replicates 1, 11, 21, 31 and 41. Rows are writers and columns are replicates."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 8
plot_replicates(1)
```

To assess whether handwriting style drifted across replicates within a session, the same 10 writers were used, with replicates 1, 11, 21, 31 and 41 plotted for session 1 (fixed). The digits were near-identical across the replicates, with little to no change in style. This indicates that a writer's handwriting within one session is usually the same. The plots for digits 0, 2, 3 and 4 are in @fig-app-replicates (Appendix A).

## Quantifying the variation

To quantify the variation between writers, across sessions and within sessions, the Euclidean distance between two images was computed over all 784 pixels. For a sample of 1,000 draws, the function picked a writer, a digit, two sessions and two replicates and formed three comparisons with the digit matched within a session (comparing replicates), across sessions (the same writer) and between writers. The three distances were compared with a Friedman test, followed by paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm's adjustment for the three comparisons. We also report the paired effect size d~z~, the mean of the paired differences divided by their standard deviation [@goulet2018]. Intervals are percentile bootstrap intervals from 2000 resamples of the draws [@efron2016].

```{r}
#| label: task1-distances
#| include: false
# Flatten each 28x28 image into one row of 784 pixel values (scaled 0-1)
x_flat <- matrix(data$images / 255, nrow = dim(data$images)[1])

# Find the row number of one specific image
get_i <- function(p, d, s, r){
  which(metadata$person_id == p & metadata$digit == d &
          metadata$session == s & metadata$replicate == r)
}

# Euclidean distance between two images (given their row numbers)
dist_img <- function(a, b) sqrt(sum((x_flat[a, ] - x_flat[b, ])^2))

set.seed(1)
n <- 1000
results <- data.frame(type = character(), digit = integer(), dist = numeric())

for (k in 1:n){
  p <- sample(1:20, 1)                  # a random writer
  d <- sample(0:4, 1)                   # a random digit
  s <- sample(1:5, 2)                   # two different sessions
  r <- sample(1:50, 2)                  # two different replicates
  q <- sample(setdiff(1:20, p), 1)      # a different writer
  
  a <- get_i(p, d, s[1], r[1])          # the reference image
  
  results[nrow(results) + 1, ] <- list("Within-session", d, dist_img(a, get_i(p, d, s[1], r[2])))
  results[nrow(results) + 1, ] <- list("Across-session", d, dist_img(a, get_i(p, d, s[2], r[2])))
  results[nrow(results) + 1, ] <- list("Between-writer", d, dist_img(a, get_i(q, d, s[1], r[2])))
}

results$type <- factor(results$type,
                       levels = c("Within-session", "Across-session", "Between-writer"))

```

```{r}
#| label: task1-stats
#| include: false
# rows = draws; the 3 distances of a draw are matched
M <- matrix(results$dist, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE,
            dimnames = list(NULL, c("Within", "Across", "Between")))
dig <- results$digit[seq(1, nrow(results), by = 3)]        # digit of each draw

set.seed(2026)
B <- 2000
boot_q <- function(v, f = mean) unname(quantile(replicate(B, f(sample(v, length(v), replace = TRUE))), c(.025, .975)))

desc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(colnames(M), function(nm) {
  v <- M[, nm]; ci <- boot_q(v)
  data.frame(Pair = nm, n = length(v), Mean = mean(v), SD = sd(v), Median = median(v),
             IQR = IQR(v), CI_low = ci[1], CI_high = ci[2])
}))
desc$Pair <- c("Within-session", "Across-session", "Between-writer")  

fr <- friedman.test(M)
kendall_w <- unname(fr$statistic) / (nrow(M) * (ncol(M) - 1))

pw <- do.call(rbind, lapply(list(c("Within", "Across"), c("Within", "Between"), c("Across", "Between")), function(p) {
  d <- M[, p[2]] - M[, p[1]]; ci <- boot_q(d)
  data.frame(Comparison = paste(p[2], "minus", p[1]), Mean_diff = mean(d), CI_low = ci[1], CI_high = ci[2],
             d_z = mean(d) / sd(d),
             p_raw = wilcox.test(M[, p[2]], M[, p[1]], paired = TRUE, exact = FALSE)$p.value)
}))
pw$p_Holm <- p.adjust(pw$p_raw, method = "holm")

ratio_by_digit <- do.call(rbind, lapply(0:4, function(dg) {
  ix <- which(dig == dg); w <- M[ix, "Within"]; a <- M[ix, "Across"]
  bs <- replicate(B, { s <- sample.int(length(ix), replace = TRUE); mean(a[s]) / mean(w[s]) })
  data.frame(Digit = dg, n = length(ix), Within = mean(w), Across = mean(a),
             Between = mean(M[ix, "Between"]),                                
             Ratio = mean(a) / mean(w),
             CI_low = unname(quantile(bs, .025)), CI_high = unname(quantile(bs, .975)))
}))

# Numbers quoted in the text
holm_txt <- if (all(pw$p_Holm < 1e-16)) "p < 1e-16" else
  sprintf("p between %s and %s", formatC(min(pw$p_Holm), format = "g", digits = 2),
          formatC(max(pw$p_Holm), format = "g", digits = 2))
frac_session <- (desc$Mean[2] - desc$Mean[1]) / (desc$Mean[3] - desc$Mean[1])
rd <- ratio_by_digit
hi_r <- which.max(rd$Ratio); lo_r <- which.min(rd$Ratio)
ratio0 <- rd$Ratio[rd$Digit == 0]
rank0 <- rank(-rd$Ratio)[rd$Digit == 0]
ord_word <- c("first", "second", "third", "fourth", "fifth")
```

Two images of the same digit by the same writer in the same session were near identical (mean distance = `r f2(desc$Mean[1])`, SD = `r f2(desc$SD[1])`), which indicates that the 50 replicates are near copies of one another. The across-session distance for the same writer had a mean of `r f2(desc$Mean[2])` and SD = `r f2(desc$SD[2])`. The highest variation was recorded between different writers (mean distance = `r f2(desc$Mean[3])`, SD = `r f2(desc$SD[3])`) (@tbl-t1-desc, @fig-t1-dist). The three distances differ clearly in the matched draws (Friedman chi-squared = `r f2(unname(fr$statistic), 1)` on `r unname(fr$parameter)` df, p `r fp(fr$p.value)`; Kendall’s W = `r f2(kendall_w)`), and all three Holm-adjusted pairwise tests give `r holm_txt` (@tbl-t1-tests).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t1-desc
#| tbl-cap: "Pixel distance between two images of the same digit, by comparison type (1,000 draws), with 95% bootstrap intervals for the mean."
knitr::kable(desc, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE, align = "lccccccc",
             col.names = c("Comparison", "Draws", "Mean", "SD", "Median", "IQR",
                           "95% CI low", "95% CI high"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-t1-dist
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of pixel distances by comparison type."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
boxplot(M, names = c("Within-session", "Across-session", "Between-writer"),
        ylab = "Pixel distance")
```

With 1,000 draws almost any difference would be significant, so the effect sizes are more informative than the p-values. The across-session minus within-session gap is `r f2(pw$Mean_diff[1])` (95% CI `r f2(pw$CI_low[1])` to `r f2(pw$CI_high[1])`; d~z~ = `r f2(pw$d_z[1])`), whereas the between-writer minus across-session gap is only `r f2(pw$Mean_diff[3])` (95% CI `r f2(pw$CI_low[3])` to `r f2(pw$CI_high[3])`; d~z~ = `r f2(pw$d_z[3])`). In practical terms, a change of session moves a writer’s digit about `r pc(frac_session, 0)` of the way to where a different writer’s digit sits ((`r f2(desc$Mean[2])` − `r f2(desc$Mean[1])`) / (`r f2(desc$Mean[3])` − `r f2(desc$Mean[1])`)). A writer is therefore only partly recognisable from the pixels of a single image, and any model has to cope with the same person looking different from one session to the next.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t1-tests
#| tbl-cap: "Paired differences between comparison types: mean difference with 95% bootstrap interval, paired effect size dz, and Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank p-values."
tab_tests <- data.frame(
  Comparison = pw$Comparison,
  `Mean difference (95% CI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", pw$Mean_diff, pw$CI_low, pw$CI_high),
  dz = round(pw$d_z, 2),
  `Holm-adjusted p` = ifelse(pw$p_Holm < 1e-16, "< 1e-16", signif(pw$p_Holm, 2)),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(tab_tests, align = "lccc")
```

The ratio of across-session to within-session distance was above 1 for every digit, and its confidence interval never came near 1 (@fig-t1-ratio, @tbl-t1-ratio). It was highest for digit `r rd$Digit[hi_r]` (`r f2(rd$Ratio[hi_r])`; within-session distance `r f2(rd$Within[hi_r])`) and lowest for digit `r rd$Digit[lo_r]` (`r f2(rd$Ratio[lo_r])`). Digit 1 is a thin stroke, so a small shift in position or slant changes which pixels are lit, which is a plausible reason for its larger ratio, although this was not tested. Digit 0 ranked `r ord_word[rank0]` of the five digits (ratio `r f2(ratio0)`). Pixel distance is a crude measure, because a small shift in a digit’s position can inflate the distance between two images of the same shape, so these numbers describe the data and do not by themselves show how well a model can separate writers.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t1-ratio
#| tbl-cap: "Mean pixel distance by digit and comparison type, and the ratio of across-session to within-session distance with a 95% bootstrap interval."
tab_digit <- data.frame(
  Digit = ratio_by_digit$Digit,
  Draws = ratio_by_digit$n,
  `Within-session` = round(ratio_by_digit$Within, 2),
  `Across-session` = round(ratio_by_digit$Across, 2),
  `Between-writer` = round(ratio_by_digit$Between, 2),
  `Across / within (95% CI)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", ratio_by_digit$Ratio,
                                       ratio_by_digit$CI_low, ratio_by_digit$CI_high),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(tab_digit, align = "cccccc")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-t1-ratio
#| fig-cap: "Ratio of across-session to within-session distance by digit, with 95% bootstrap intervals. The dashed line marks a ratio of 1."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
plot(ratio_by_digit$Digit, ratio_by_digit$Ratio, pch = 19, xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Digit", ylab = "Across / within distance",
     ylim = range(c(1, ratio_by_digit$CI_low, ratio_by_digit$CI_high)))
axis(1, at = 0:4)
arrows(ratio_by_digit$Digit, ratio_by_digit$CI_low,
       ratio_by_digit$Digit, ratio_by_digit$CI_high,
       angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.05)
abline(h = 1, lty = 2)
```

This has a consequence for how the data are split in the next tasks. A random split would put near-copies of the same image in both the training and the test set, so it would measure memory more than generalisation.

# Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)

Task 2 treats writer identification as a 20-class classification problem: the input is an image and the output is the writer's ID. All 20 writers appear in the training data, so this is identification of known writers, not verification of unknown ones.

**Uncertainty.** The 50 replicates within a writer, digit and session are near copies, so images are not independent and a binomial interval treats the test set as holding more information than it does. We report the exact Clopper-Pearson interval for reference [@agresti2019], but base our uncertainty on a cluster bootstrap: whole writer-digit groups (100 in the test session, 20 per digit) are resampled with replacement and the accuracy is recomputed 2000 times, which keeps the dependence inside each group [@efron2016; @saravanan2020]. Differences between digits are tested with a Friedman test, using each writer's accuracy on each digit as the unit and the writers as blocks.

```{r}
#| label: task2-split
# Free memory 
if (exists("x_flat")) rm(x_flat)
invisible(gc())
seed_all(1)  

x <- data$images / 255
y_person <- data$metadata$person_id - 1L
data$images <- NULL   # the raw images are not needed again 
invisible(gc())

# Splitting data by session. Session 1-3 for training, session 4 for validation and session 5 for testing

# Picking rows by session
meta <- data$metadata # this is the table with one row per image

train_rows <- which(meta$session %in% 1:3) # row numbers of session 1-3

val_rows <- which(meta$session == 4)
test_rows <- which(meta$session == 5)

# images and labels
x_train <- x[train_rows, , , , drop = FALSE]
y_train <- y_person[train_rows]

x_val <- x[val_rows, , , , drop = FALSE]
y_val <- y_person[val_rows]

x_test <- x[test_rows, , , , drop = FALSE]
y_test <- y_person[test_rows]

```

**Split.** We split by session: sessions 1 to 3 for training (15 000 images), session 4 for validation and session 5 for testing (5 000 images each). This asks whether a model trained on a person's earlier writing recognises them in a later session, and it stops near-identical replicates (@sec-task1) from straddling the training and test sets. Random splitting of records that share a source is known to give optimistic results: random cross-validation on structured data underestimates predictive error because the dependence between records is ignored [@roberts2017], and @saeb2017 make the same case for subject-wise versus record-wise validation. Leakage between training and test data is a wider cause of over-optimistic results in machine-learning studies [@kapoor2023]. As a check, we also trained the same model on a random split (15 000 images for training, 5 000 for validation).

```{r}
#| label: task2-cnn
#| output: false
# CNN Model building
seed_all(1)   # fixed start weights, dropout masks and batch order for the baseline CNN
model <- keras_model_sequential(input_shape = c(28, 28, 1)) |>
  layer_conv_2d(filters = 32, kernel_size = 3, activation = "relu") |> #keeps positive signals only
  layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = 2) |>       #shrinks the image by half
  layer_conv_2d(filters = 64, kernel_size = 3, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = 2) |>
  layer_flatten() |>
  layer_dense(units = 64, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_dropout(rate = 0.3) |>
  layer_dense(units = 20, activation = "softmax")

# Compiling and training
model |> compile(
  loss = "sparse_categorical_crossentropy",
  optimizer = "adam",
  metrics = "accuracy"
)

history <- model |> fit(
  x_train, y_train,
  epochs = 10,
  batch_size = 128,
  validation_data = list(x_val, y_val),
  verbose = 2   # one line per epoch keeps the rendered report tidy
)
```

```{r}
#| label: task2-leakage
#| output: false
# Checking for leakage using random split
set.seed(123)
idx <- sample(nrow(x))
rand_train <- idx[1:15000]
rand_val   <- idx[15001:20000]

x_tr_rand <- x[rand_train, , , , drop = FALSE]
y_tr_rand <- y_person[rand_train]
x_va_rand <- x[rand_val, , , , drop = FALSE]
y_va_rand <- y_person[rand_val]

seed_all(1)   # same seed as the baseline CNN, so the two models differ only in the split
model_rand <- keras_model_sequential(input_shape = c(28, 28, 1)) |>
  layer_conv_2d(filters = 32, kernel_size = 3, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = 2) |>
  layer_conv_2d(filters = 64, kernel_size = 3, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = 2) |>
  layer_flatten() |>
  layer_dense(units = 64, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_dropout(rate = 0.3) |>
  layer_dense(units = 20, activation = "softmax")

model_rand |> compile(
  loss = "sparse_categorical_crossentropy",
  optimizer = "adam",
  metrics = "accuracy"
)

# The objects defined above are x_tr_rand / y_tr_rand / x_va_rand / y_va_rand.
history_rand <- model_rand |> fit(
  x_tr_rand, y_tr_rand,
  epochs = 10,
  batch_size = 128,
  validation_data = list(x_va_rand, y_va_rand),
  verbose = 2
)

# The random-split copies of the images are no longer needed
rm(x_tr_rand, x_va_rand); invisible(gc())
```

**Model.** The CNN has two convolution and max-pooling blocks (32 and then 64 filters of size 3 × 3), which learn local stroke patterns and then combine them [@goodfellow2016; @gu2018]. These are followed by rectified linear activations, a flatten layer, a dense layer of 64 units with 30% dropout (which randomly switches off units during training to reduce overfitting) and a softmax output of 20 units [@goodfellow2016]. We trained with sparse categorical cross-entropy and the Adam optimiser for 10 epochs with batches of 128 [@goodfellow2016; @chollet2022].

```{r}
#| label: task2-evaluate
#| output: false
# Accuracy by digit
pred  <- model |> predict(x_val, verbose = 0)
pred_class <- max.col(pred) - 1L
meta_val  <- meta[val_rows, ]

acc_by_digit <- tapply(pred_class == y_val, meta_val$digit, mean)
acc_by_digit

# Evaluating the model
# test accuracy
model |> evaluate(x_test, y_test, verbose = 0)

# Accuracy by digit on test set
pred_test <- model |> predict(x_test, verbose = 0)
pred_class_test <- max.col(pred_test) - 1L
meta_test <- meta[test_rows, ]

acc_by_digit_test <- tapply(pred_class_test == y_test, meta_test$digit, mean)
acc_by_digit_test

# Results in a table
results_table <- data.frame(
  Digit = 0:4,
  Validation = round(100 * as.numeric(acc_by_digit), 1),
  Test = round(100 * as.numeric(acc_by_digit_test), 1)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t2-valtest
#| tbl-cap: "Accuracy by digit on the validation (session 4) and test (session 5) sets."
knitr::kable(results_table,
             col.names = c("Digit", "Validation accuracy (%)", "Test accuracy (%)"))
```

**What the measures capture.** Accuracy is the proportion of images assigned to the right writer. Chance is 1/20 = 5%, because the 20 writers are equally represented. The confusion matrix shows which writers are mistaken for which, that is, whose handwriting looks alike to the model. Accuracy by digit asks how much writer information a single digit carries.

**Performance by digit.**

```{r}
#| label: task2-digit-text
#| include: false
# Numbers for the "Performance by digit" paragraph (all from results_table)
rt <- results_table
hi_t <- rt$Digit[which.max(rt$Test)];       lo_t <- rt$Digit[which.min(rt$Test)]
hi_v <- rt$Digit[which.max(rt$Validation)]; lo_v <- rt$Digit[which.min(rt$Validation)]
top2_t <- sort(rt$Digit[order(rt$Test, decreasing = TRUE)[1:2]])
top2_v <- sort(rt$Digit[order(rt$Validation, decreasing = TRUE)[1:2]])
top2_txt <- if (identical(top2_t, top2_v))
  sprintf("The two highest digits (%s) were the same in both sets.", join_and(top2_t)) else
  sprintf("The two highest digits differed between the sets (test: %s; validation: %s).", join_and(top2_t), join_and(top2_v))
chg <- abs(rt$Test - rt$Validation)
low3_t <- rt$Digit[order(rt$Test)[1:3]]
low3_spread <- diff(range(rt$Test[match(low3_t, rt$Digit)]))
```

@tbl-t2-valtest shows the validation (session 4) and test (session 5) accuracy for each digit, using 1 000 images per digit in each session. On the test set the highest accuracy (`r f1(max(rt$Test))`%) was for digit `r hi_t` and the lowest (`r f1(min(rt$Test))`%) was for digit `r lo_t`, a difference of `r f1(max(rt$Test) - min(rt$Test))` percentage points. Every digit is far above the 5% expected by chance when identifying among 20 writers, so each digit contains information about who wrote it.

On the validation set the highest accuracy (`r f1(max(rt$Validation))`%) was for digit `r hi_v` and the lowest (`r f1(min(rt$Validation))`%) was for digit `r lo_v`. Between the two sets, accuracy for the digits changed by `r f1(min(chg))` to `r f1(max(chg))` percentage points, with the largest change for digit `r rt$Digit[which.max(chg)]`. `r top2_txt` The three lowest digits on the test set (`r join_and(low3_t)`) lie within `r f1(low3_spread)` percentage points of each other, so their order is not reliable. In this run all digits carry writer information above chance. Digit `r hi_t` had the highest test accuracy, although the differences between digits are not statistically reliable (see below).

```{r}
#| label: task2-stats
#| include: false
# Statistics behind the CNN results
set.seed(2026)
B <- 2000
correct <- pred_class_test == y_test

# Cluster bootstrap: resample whole clusters (e.g. writer x digit groups) with replacement
boot_cluster <- function(correct, cluster, B = 2000) {
  k_c <- tapply(correct, cluster, sum); n_c <- tapply(correct, cluster, length); K <- length(k_c)
  bs <- replicate(B, { i <- sample.int(K, K, replace = TRUE); sum(k_c[i]) / sum(n_c[i]) })
  unname(quantile(bs, c(.025, .975)))
}

n_test <- length(correct); k_test <- sum(correct)
cp_all   <- binom.test(k_test, n_test)$conf.int
boot_all <- boot_cluster(correct, paste(meta_test$person_id, meta_test$digit))

last <- function(v) v[length(v)]
acc_summary <- data.frame(
  Split = c(rep("Session split", 3), rep("Random split", 2)),
  Evaluated_on = c("Training (sessions 1-3), last epoch", "Validation (session 4)", "Test (session 5)",
                   "Training (random), last epoch", "Validation (random)"),
  n = c(length(train_rows), length(val_rows), n_test, length(rand_train), length(rand_val)),
  Accuracy = c(last(history$metrics$accuracy), last(history$metrics$val_accuracy), k_test / n_test,
               last(history_rand$metrics$accuracy), last(history_rand$metrics$val_accuracy)),
  CP_low = c(NA, NA, cp_all[1], NA, NA), CP_high = c(NA, NA, cp_all[2], NA, NA),
  Boot_low = c(NA, NA, boot_all[1], NA, NA), Boot_high = c(NA, NA, boot_all[2], NA, NA))

# Accuracy by digit (clusters = writers within a digit)
digit_stats <- do.call(rbind, lapply(0:4, function(dg) {
  ix <- meta_test$digit == dg; cr <- correct[ix]
  cp <- binom.test(sum(cr), length(cr))$conf.int
  bc <- boot_cluster(cr, meta_test$person_id[ix])
  data.frame(Digit = dg, n = length(cr), Accuracy = mean(cr), CP_low = cp[1], CP_high = cp[2],
             Boot_low = bc[1], Boot_high = bc[2])
}))

# Do digits differ? Friedman test with writers as blocks
cl <- aggregate(correct ~ person + digit,
                data = data.frame(correct = correct, person = meta_test$person_id, digit = meta_test$digit),
                FUN = mean)
acc_mat <- with(cl, tapply(correct, list(person, digit), mean))
fr2 <- friedman.test(acc_mat)
w2 <- unname(fr2$statistic) / (nrow(acc_mat) * (ncol(acc_mat) - 1))

# Accuracy by writer
writer_acc <- data.frame(Writer = as.integer(names(tapply(correct, meta_test$person_id, mean))),
                         Accuracy = as.numeric(tapply(correct, meta_test$person_id, mean)))

# Confusion matrix (rows = true writer, normalised by row)
cm <- table(truth = factor(y_test, levels = 0:19), predicted = factor(pred_class_test, levels = 0:19))
cm_df <- as.data.frame(cm)
cm_df$prop <- cm_df$Freq / ave(cm_df$Freq, cm_df$truth, FUN = sum)
cm_df$truth <- factor(as.integer(as.character(cm_df$truth)) + 1L, levels = 1:20)
cm_df$predicted <- factor(as.integer(as.character(cm_df$predicted)) + 1L, levels = 1:20)
off <- unclass(cm); diag(off) <- 0
top <- head(order(off, decreasing = TRUE), 5)
top_conf <- data.frame(True_writer = row(off)[top] , Predicted_as = col(off)[top], Images = off[top],
                       Share_of_true_writers_images = off[top] / rowSums(unclass(cm))[row(off)[top]])
```

```{r}
#| label: task2-numbers
#| include: false
# Every number quoted in the Task 2 text comes from the objects below
train_acc    <- last(history$metrics$accuracy)
val_acc_last <- last(history$metrics$val_accuracy)
val_acc_rng  <- range(history$metrics$val_accuracy)
val_loss_1   <- history$metrics$val_loss[1]
val_loss_end <- last(history$metrics$val_loss)
rand_val_acc <- last(history_rand$metrics$val_accuracy)
test_acc     <- k_test / n_test
gap_pts      <- 100 * (rand_val_acc - test_acc)
best_digit   <- digit_stats$Digit[which.max(digit_stats$Accuracy)]
tc1 <- top_conf[1, ]
n_per_writer <- unname(rowSums(unclass(cm))[tc1$True_writer])
tc2 <- top_conf[2, ]
rev_share <- unname(off[tc2$Predicted_as, tc2$True_writer] / rowSums(unclass(cm))[tc2$Predicted_as])
second_txt <- sprintf("Writer %d was mistaken for writer %d in %s of cases, and writer %d for writer %d in %s, %s.",
                      tc2$True_writer, tc2$Predicted_as, pc(tc2$Share_of_true_writers_images, 0),
                      tc2$Predicted_as, tc2$True_writer, pc(rev_share, 0),
                      if (rev_share >= 0.2) "so those two seem to write alike in session 5"
                      else "so this confusion runs mostly in one direction")
```

## What Task 2 tells us

The CNN fitted the training sessions almost perfectly (`r pc(train_acc)` accuracy after 10 epochs) but identified the writer correctly in only `r pc(test_acc)` of the test images from the unseen session 5 (@tbl-t2-summary). The exact Clopper-Pearson interval is `r pc(cp_all[1])` to `r pc(cp_all[2])`, but this treats the 5 000 images as independent, which they are not. The cluster bootstrap, which resamples whole writer-digit groups, gives a much wider interval of `r pc(boot_all[1])` to `r pc(boot_all[2])` [@saravanan2020], so the honest statement is that test accuracy is roughly `r pc(boot_all[1], 0)` to `r pc(boot_all[2], 0)`. Either way it is far above the 5% expected by chance, and far below the training accuracy. The learning curves show where the gap comes from (@fig-t2-curves). Validation accuracy stays between about `r pc(val_acc_rng[1], 0)` and `r pc(val_acc_rng[2], 0)` from the first epoch, while the validation loss rises from `r f2(val_loss_1)` to `r f2(val_loss_end)` as the training loss falls. The network is becoming more confident without becoming more correct on a new session, which is what overfitting looks like [@goodfellow2016]. We did not use early stopping here, so the test result is for the model after 10 epochs.

The random split is the contrast that matters. The same network reached `r pc(rand_val_acc)` validation accuracy within ten epochs when the images were shuffled across training and validation. That near-perfect score is not evidence of a better model. It is the leakage that Task 1 predicted, because the validation images have near-copies in the training set (the within-session distance was only `r f2(desc$Mean[1])`). The gap of about `r round(gap_pts)` points between the random split (`r pc(rand_val_acc)`) and the session-split test (`r pc(test_acc)`) shows how much a random split would have overstated performance [@roberts2017; @saeb2017].

Accuracy was similar across digits (`r pc(min(digit_stats$Accuracy))` to `r pc(max(digit_stats$Accuracy))`), with digit `r best_digit` highest at `r pc(max(digit_stats$Accuracy))`. The cluster-bootstrap intervals for the five digits overlap almost completely (@fig-t2-digit, @tbl-t2-digit), and a Friedman test across digits with writers as blocks gives chi-squared = `r f2(unname(fr2$statistic), 2)` on `r unname(fr2$parameter)` df, p `r fp(fr2$p.value)` (Kendall's W = `r f2(w2)`). The data therefore give little support for saying that some digits identify writers better than others, and the digit `r best_digit` result should be treated as a hint at most.

The errors are concentrated in particular writers more than in particular digits (@fig-t2-writer, @fig-t2-confusion). The clearest case is writer `r tc1$True_writer`: `r tc1$Images` of that writer’s `r n_per_writer` test images (`r pc(tc1$Share_of_true_writers_images, 0)`) were assigned to writer `r tc1$Predicted_as` (@tbl-t2-confusions). `r second_txt` We only report this as an observation, because the matrix shows that it happens but not why.

In real-world terms, the model is given one digit from a known writer in a session it has not seen and must say who wrote it. The overall test accuracy of `r pc(test_acc)` means that, out of 100 new digits from known writers, about `r round(100 * test_acc)` are assigned to the right writer and about `r 100 - round(100 * test_acc)` to the wrong one, so the model has learned real writer information but still makes many mistakes. The results do not show how it would handle writers it has not seen, since it can only choose among the 20 known writers, or real handwriting, since the images are simulated.

# Siamese network

Task 3 changes the question. Instead of naming the writer, the network judges whether two images were written by the same person, so it can be applied to writers it has never seen (verification instead of identification). We use a Siamese network [@chicco2021]: one encoder turns each image into a 16-number embedding, the same encoder (with shared weights) is applied to both images in a pair, and the model outputs the Euclidean distance between the two embeddings. The encoder has two convolution and max-pooling stages (16 and 32 filters), global average pooling and a dense layer of 16 units.

**Training examples.** Positive pairs show the same writer and negative pairs show different writers, in roughly equal numbers. Both images in a pair show the same digit; otherwise the network could answer "different writer" whenever the digits differ, instead of comparing handwriting. We split by writer before building pairs: writers 1 to 14 for training (8 000 pairs), 15 to 17 for validation (2 000 pairs) and 18 to 20 for testing (2 000 pairs). Pairs are built only inside one part, so no image or writer appears in more than one part. Because the aim is to compare people, testing on unseen writers is the appropriate kind of generalisation.

**Loss.** We use the contrastive loss, which Siamese networks commonly use to learn distances [@chicco2021]. With $D$ the distance between the two embeddings, $y = 1$ for a same-writer pair and $m = 1$ the margin,

$$L = y\,D^{2} + (1 - y)\,\max(0,\; m - D)^{2}.$$

Same-writer pairs are pulled together, and different-writer pairs are pushed apart only while they are closer than the margin. Some authors write the same loss with the labels reversed (0 for similar pairs); we follow the convention of the course slides. We optimised with Adam and early stopping on the validation loss, keeping the best weights.

**Evaluation.** The network outputs a distance, so a decision rule is needed: a pair is called "same writer" if its distance is below a threshold. We chose the threshold on the validation pairs to maximise balanced accuracy, the mean of the true match rate and the true non-match rate, which does not favour the more common pair type [@luque2019], and then fixed it for the test pairs. Because one threshold is one operating point, we also report the ROC curve, which plots the true match rate against the false match rate over all thresholds, and the area under it (AUC), the probability that a randomly chosen same-writer pair has a smaller distance than a randomly chosen different-writer pair. Intervals are percentile bootstrap intervals over test pairs [@efron2016] and exact Clopper-Pearson intervals for rates [@agresti2019]. These intervals reflect the sampling of pairs only. The pairs reuse a small set of images from three writers, so we also report results for each test writer separately.

## Pair construction

```{r}
#| label: task3-pairs
seed_all(1)   

# 1. Split by WRITER first, so validation/test writers are never seen in training
tr_ids <- which(meta$person_id %in% 1:14)
va_ids <- which(meta$person_id %in% 15:17)
te_ids <- which(meta$person_id %in% 18:20)

# 2. Build pairs INSIDE one part. About half are same-writer (label 1), half
#    different-writer (label 0). Both images in a pair show the SAME digit, so
#    the model has to compare handwriting, not digit shape.
make_pairs <- function(ids, n){
  a <- sample(ids, n, replace = TRUE)
  same <- runif(n) < 0.5
  b <- integer(n)
  for (k in seq_len(n)){
    i <- a[k]
    pool <- ids[meta$digit[ids] == meta$digit[i]]
    pool <- if (same[k]) pool[meta$person_id[pool] == meta$person_id[i]]
            else         pool[meta$person_id[pool] != meta$person_id[i]]
    pool <- setdiff(pool, i)
    b[k] <- pool[sample.int(length(pool), 1)]
  }
  cbind(a, b)
}
make_batch <- function(p) list(
  left  = x[p[, 1], , , , drop = FALSE],
  right = x[p[, 2], , , , drop = FALSE],
  y     = matrix(as.numeric(meta$person_id[p[, 1]] == meta$person_id[p[, 2]]), ncol = 1))

tr_pairs <- make_pairs(tr_ids, 8000)
va_pairs <- make_pairs(va_ids, 2000)
te_pairs <- make_pairs(te_ids, 2000)   # keep the indices so test pairs can be analysed later
train <- make_batch(tr_pairs)
valid <- make_batch(va_pairs)
test  <- make_batch(te_pairs)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-t3-pairs
#| tbl-cap: "Composition of the pair sets. Images are never shared between sets because the split is by writer."
pair_sets <- list(Training = tr_pairs, Validation = va_pairs, Test = te_pairs)
comp <- data.frame(
  Set = names(pair_sets),
  Writers = c("1-14", "15-17", "18-20"),
  Pairs = sapply(pair_sets, nrow),
  Same_writer_share = sapply(pair_sets, function(p) mean(meta$person_id[p[, 1]] == meta$person_id[p[, 2]])),
  Same_digit_in_pair = sapply(pair_sets, function(p) all(meta$digit[p[, 1]] == meta$digit[p[, 2]])),
  Distinct_images = sapply(pair_sets, function(p) length(unique(c(p)))))
knitr::kable(comp, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Set", "Writers", "Pairs", "Share same-writer", "Same digit in every pair", "Distinct images"))
```

```{r}
#| label: task3-model
#| output: false
seed_all(1)   # fixed start weights and batch order for the Siamese network
# 3. Shared encoder: the same layers (same weights) are used for both images
img_in <- layer_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))
z <- img_in |>
  layer_conv_2d(16, 3, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_max_pooling_2d(2) |>
  layer_conv_2d(32, 3, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_global_average_pooling_2d() |>
  layer_dense(16)
encoder <- keras_model(img_in, z)

# 4. Siamese model: output = Euclidean distance between the two embeddings
left_in  <- layer_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))
right_in <- layer_input(shape = c(28, 28, 1))
emb_left  <- encoder(left_in)
emb_right <- encoder(right_in)
distance  <- op_sqrt(op_sum(op_square(emb_left - emb_right), axis = 2, keepdims = TRUE) + 1e-7)
siamese <- keras_model(list(left_in, right_in), distance)


# 5. Contrastive loss with margin 1:
#    same pairs (y = 1) are pulled together (loss D^2);
#    different pairs (y = 0) are pushed apart until D >= 1, then left alone.
contrastive_loss <- function(y, d) {
  op_mean(y * op_square(d) + (1 - y) * op_square(op_maximum(1 - d, 0)))
}
siamese |> compile(optimizer = optimizer_adam(1e-3), loss = contrastive_loss)

history_siam <- siamese |> fit(
  list(train$left, train$right), train$y,
  validation_data = list(list(valid$left, valid$right), valid$y),
  epochs = 12, batch_size = 64, verbose = 2,
  callbacks = list(callback_early_stopping(monitor = "val_loss", patience = 2,
                                           restore_best_weights = TRUE))
)
```

## Threshold, test performance and breakdowns

```{r}
#| label: task3-eval
#| output: false
# 6. Choose the distance threshold on VALIDATION pairs (not on test)
valid_distance <- as.numeric(predict(siamese, list(valid$left, valid$right), verbose = 0))
valid_same <- valid$y[, 1] == 1

# balanced accuracy = average of (true match rate) and (true non-match rate)
bal_acc <- function(d, same, cut){
  pred_same <- d < cut
  (mean(pred_same[same]) + mean(!pred_same[!same])) / 2
}
# AUC = P(a same-writer pair has a smaller distance than a different-writer pair)
auc_dist <- function(d, same){
  r <- rank(d); n1 <- sum(same); n0 <- sum(!same)
  1 - (sum(r[same]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}

cuts <- seq(min(valid_distance), max(valid_distance), length.out = 200)
scores <- sapply(cuts, function(cc) bal_acc(valid_distance, valid_same, cc))
threshold <- cuts[which.max(scores)]
c(threshold = threshold, validation_balanced_accuracy = max(scores))

# 7. Evaluate once on TEST pairs (new writers), threshold fixed from validation
test_distance <- as.numeric(predict(siamese, list(test$left, test$right), verbose = 0))
test_same <- test$y[, 1] == 1
pred_same <- test_distance < threshold

c(test_balanced_accuracy = bal_acc(test_distance, test_same, threshold),
  true_match_rate        = mean(pred_same[test_same]),
  true_non_match_rate    = mean(!pred_same[!test_same]))

table(truth = test_same, predicted = pred_same)
```

```{r}
#| label: task3-stats
#| include: false
# statistics behind the Siamese results
set.seed(2026)
B <- 1000
n_pairs <- length(test_same)

bal_hat <- bal_acc(test_distance, test_same, threshold)
auc_hat <- auc_dist(test_distance, test_same)
boot_t3 <- t(replicate(B, {
  i <- sample.int(n_pairs, replace = TRUE)
  c(bal = bal_acc(test_distance[i], test_same[i], threshold), auc = auc_dist(test_distance[i], test_same[i]))
}))
tmr_k <- sum(pred_same[test_same]);   tmr_n <- sum(test_same)
tnr_k <- sum(!pred_same[!test_same]); tnr_n <- sum(!test_same)
cp1 <- binom.test(tmr_k, tmr_n)$conf.int; cp0 <- binom.test(tnr_k, tnr_n)$conf.int
t3_metrics <- data.frame(
  Measure = c("Balanced accuracy", "True match rate (same writer accepted)",
              "True non-match rate (different writer rejected)", "AUC"),
  Estimate = c(bal_hat, tmr_k / tmr_n, tnr_k / tnr_n, auc_hat),
  CI_low  = c(quantile(boot_t3[, "bal"], .025), cp1[1], cp0[1], quantile(boot_t3[, "auc"], .025)),
  CI_high = c(quantile(boot_t3[, "bal"], .975), cp1[2], cp0[2], quantile(boot_t3[, "auc"], .975)),
  Interval = c("Bootstrap", "Clopper-Pearson", "Clopper-Pearson", "Bootstrap"))

# confusion counts
t3_conf <- data.frame(
  Truth = c("Same writer", "Different writers"),
  Accepted_as_same = c(tmr_k, tnr_n - tnr_k), Rejected_as_different = c(tmr_n - tmr_k, tnr_k))

# ROC curve
roc_cuts <- c(-Inf, sort(unique(test_distance)), Inf)
roc <- data.frame(fpr = sapply(roc_cuts, function(cc) mean(test_distance[!test_same] < cc)),
                  tpr = sapply(roc_cuts, function(cc) mean(test_distance[test_same]  < cc)))

# Same-session versus different-session pairs
same_session <- meta$session[te_pairs[, 1]] == meta$session[te_pairs[, 2]]
cond <- function(cls_same, sess_same) {
  ix <- test_same == cls_same & same_session == sess_same
  k <- if (cls_same) sum(pred_same[ix]) else sum(!pred_same[ix])
  cp <- if (sum(ix) > 0) binom.test(k, sum(ix))$conf.int else c(NA, NA)
  data.frame(Pair_class = if (cls_same) "Same writer" else "Different writers",
             Sessions = if (sess_same) "Same session" else "Different sessions",
             n = sum(ix), Correct = k, Rate = if (sum(ix) > 0) k / sum(ix) else NA, CI_low = cp[1], CI_high = cp[2])
}
sess_tab <- rbind(cond(TRUE, TRUE), cond(TRUE, FALSE), cond(FALSE, TRUE), cond(FALSE, FALSE))
fisher_p <- function(cls_same) {
  a <- sess_tab[sess_tab$Pair_class == if (cls_same) "Same writer" else "Different writers", ]
  if (any(a$n == 0)) return(NA_real_)
  fisher.test(matrix(c(a$Correct[1], a$n[1] - a$Correct[1], a$Correct[2], a$n[2] - a$Correct[2]), 2))$p.value
}
p_same_writer_sessions <- fisher_p(TRUE); p_diff_writer_sessions <- fisher_p(FALSE)

# By anchor writer (writer of the first image in each test pair)
anchor <- meta$person_id[te_pairs[, 1]]
by_writer <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sort(unique(anchor)), function(w) {
  ix <- anchor == w
  tmr <- mean(pred_same[ix & test_same]); tnr <- mean(!pred_same[ix & !test_same])
  data.frame(Writer = w, Pairs = sum(ix), Same_pairs = sum(ix & test_same),
             TMR = tmr, TNR = tnr, Bal_acc = (tmr + tnr) / 2, AUC = auc_dist(test_distance[ix], test_same[ix]))
}))

# By digit (the digit is the same in both images)
pair_digit <- meta$digit[te_pairs[, 1]]
by_digit <- do.call(rbind, lapply(0:4, function(dg) {
  ix <- which(pair_digit == dg)
  bs <- replicate(500, { i <- sample(ix, replace = TRUE); bal_acc(test_distance[i], test_same[i], threshold) })
  data.frame(Digit = dg, Pairs = length(ix), Bal_acc = bal_acc(test_distance[ix], test_same[ix], threshold),
             CI_low = unname(quantile(bs, .025)), CI_high = unname(quantile(bs, .975)))
}))

# Numbers quoted in the text
val_bal    <- max(scores)
tmr_hat    <- tmr_k / tmr_n
tnr_hat    <- tnr_k / tnr_n
bal_ci     <- unname(quantile(boot_t3[, "bal"], c(.025, .975)))
auc_ci     <- unname(quantile(boot_t3[, "auc"], c(.025, .975)))
best_ep    <- which.min(history_siam$metrics$val_loss)
best_vloss <- min(history_siam$metrics$val_loss)
stop_ep    <- length(history_siam$metrics$val_loss)
ss <- sess_tab   # 1 same-writer/same-session, 2 same-writer/different-sessions, 3 different-writer/same-session, 4 different-writer/different-sessions
share_same_session <- ss$n[1] / (ss$n[1] + ss$n[2])
bal_diff_sess <- mean(c(ss$Rate[2], ss$Rate[4]))   # balanced accuracy on different-session pairs only
```

## What Task 3 tells us

On three writers the network never saw during training, the Siamese network separated same-writer from different-writer pairs well. At the distance threshold of `r f2(threshold)` chosen on the validation pairs, balanced accuracy on the test pairs was `r f3(bal_hat)` (95% bootstrap CI `r f3(bal_ci[1])` to `r f3(bal_ci[2])`), with a true match rate of `r f3(tmr_hat)` and a true non-match rate of `r f3(tnr_hat)` (@tbl-t3-metrics, @tbl-t3-confusion). The AUC of `r f3(auc_hat)` (95% CI `r f3(auc_ci[1])` to `r f3(auc_ci[2])`) shows that the ranking of pairs by distance is good over all thresholds, not only at the one chosen (@fig-t3-roc, @fig-t3-dist). Early stopping kept the weights from epoch `r best_ep` (validation loss `r f3(best_vloss)`) and stopped at epoch `r stop_ep` (@fig-t3-loss). The test balanced accuracy is `r ifelse(bal_hat > val_bal, "higher", "lower")` than the `r f3(val_bal)` seen on the validation pairs at the chosen threshold. With only three writers in each of the two sets, that difference could come from which writers happened to be in each set, so we do not read anything into it.

Task 1 predicted that pairs from different sessions would be harder, and the session breakdown shows this for same-writer pairs (@tbl-t3-session). Of the `r ss$n[1]` same-writer pairs from the same session, `r ss$Correct[1]` were accepted (`r pc0(ss$Rate[1])`, exact CI `r pc0(ss$CI_low[1])` to `r pc0(ss$CI_high[1])`), against `r pc0(ss$Rate[2])` (`r ss$Correct[2]` of `r ss$n[2]`) for same-writer pairs from different sessions (Fisher exact p `r fp(p_same_writer_sessions)`). For different-writer pairs there was no clear session effect (`r pc0(ss$Rate[3])` against `r pc0(ss$Rate[4])`, p `r fp(p_diff_writer_sessions)`). In other words, the network is least sure when asked to connect two sessions of one person, which is the case the application cares about. The same-session figure is also not independent evidence, since those images are near-copies.

Performance differed a little between the three test writers (balanced accuracy `r f3(by_writer$Bal_acc[1])`, `r f3(by_writer$Bal_acc[2])` and `r f3(by_writer$Bal_acc[3])` for writers 18, 19 and 20; @tbl-t3-writer), and between digits (@fig-t3-digit). With three writers and the pairs sharing images (2 000 test pairs use `r sp(comp$Distinct_images[3])` distinct images, @tbl-t3-pairs), the intervals in @tbl-t3-metrics are likely to be too narrow, so they should be read as the lower bound on the uncertainty.

# Train, validation and test strategy {#sec-strategy}

For the CNN we split by session. Sessions 1 to 3 (15 000 images) were used for training, session 4 (5 000 images) for validation and session 5 (5 000 images) for testing, so each writer, digit and session group of 50 images sits in exactly one set. The training set fits the weights, the validation set is used to monitor and compare models, and the test set was used once, for the final result.

We split by session and not at random because the 50 replicates of a writer, digit and session are near copies of each other (Task 1: mean within-session distance `r f2(desc$Mean[1])`). In a random split, near copies of the test images sit in the training set, so the model is rewarded for remembering and not for generalising. This is the leakage problem that is known for grouped data [@roberts2017; @kapoor2023]. Splitting by session keeps each group of copies on one side. We did not split by writer for the CNN, because a classifier with 20 output classes can only name writers it was trained on.

We checked this with a random split of the same size. Validation accuracy was `r pc(val_acc_last)` on the session split and `r pc(rand_val_acc)` on the random split, so the random split overstated performance by about `r round(100 * (rand_val_acc - val_acc_last))` percentage points. The session-split results still have limits: all 20 writers are in the training data, the images are simulated, and everything rests on one test session, so another session could give a different accuracy.

For the Siamese network we split by writer before making pairs: writers 1 to 14 (8 000 pairs) for training, 15 to 17 (2 000 pairs) for validation and 18 to 20 (2 000 pairs) for testing. No writer or image appears in more than one set, so the test measures verification of unseen people, which is a different question from the CNN's. The threshold was chosen on the validation pairs and fixed before testing. The validation pairs were also used for early stopping, so the validation score (`r f3(val_bal)`) is slightly optimistic. The test score was `r f3(bal_hat)`, and the gap between the two most likely reflects which writers fell in each set, since each set has only a few writers.

Two features of the Siamese test need care. First, only `r pc(share_same_session, 0)` of the same-writer test pairs come from one session, but those pairs are near copies and were always accepted (`r ss$Correct[1]` of `r ss$n[1]`), which lifts the overall score. On different-session pairs alone the balanced accuracy was `r f3(bal_diff_sess)`, against `r f3(bal_hat)` overall. Second, the 2 000 test pairs reuse `r sp(comp$Distinct_images[3])` images from three writers, so pair-based intervals are too narrow, and the balanced accuracy ranged from `r f3(min(by_writer$Bal_acc))` to `r f3(max(by_writer$Bal_acc))` across the three writers (@tbl-t3-writer). Finally, because the images are simulated and each pair shows one digit, performance on real handwriting or on pairs of different digits may be lower.

# Hyperparameter optimisation

```{r}
#| label: hyper-fit
#| output: false
seed_all(1)
#model builder (base)
build_cnn <- function(filters = 32, dropout = 0.3, lr = 0.001){
  m <- keras_model_sequential(input_shape = c(28, 28, 1)) |>
    layer_conv_2d(filters = filters, kernel_size = 3, activation = "relu") |>
    layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = 2) |>
    layer_conv_2d(filters = filters * 2, kernel_size = 3, activation = "relu") |>
    layer_max_pooling_2d(pool_size = 2) |>
    layer_flatten() |>
    layer_dense(units = 64, activation = "relu") |>
    layer_dropout(rate = dropout) |>
    layer_dense(units = 20, activation = "softmax")
  m |> compile(
    loss = "sparse_categorical_crossentropy",
    optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = lr),
    metrics = "accuracy"
  )
  m
}
# varying 3 learning rates and 3 filter sizes = 9 model combinations 
grid <- expand.grid(lr = c(0.0003, 0.001, 0.003),
                    filters = c(16, 32, 64))
is_base <- grid$lr == 0.001 & grid$filters == 32    
epochs_used <- 10


#modelling
models <- vector("list", nrow(grid))

for (g in seq_len(nrow(grid))){
  if (is_base[g]){
    models[[g]] <- model        #trained baseline CNN (learning rate = 0.001) Task 2
    next
  }
  seed_all(1)   # same seed for every grid model
  models[[g]] <- build_cnn(filters = grid$filters[g], lr = grid$lr[g])
  models[[g]] |> fit(x_train, y_train,
                     epochs = epochs_used, batch_size = 128, verbose = 0)
  cat("trained", g, "of", nrow(grid), "\n")
}


#validation accuracy overall and by digit, for every model
meta_val  <- meta[val_rows, ]
digit_acc <- matrix(NA, nrow(grid), 5,
                    dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("Digit_", 0:4)))
grid$val_acc <- NA

for (g in seq_len(nrow(grid))){
  pred_class <- max.col(models[[g]] |> predict(x_val, verbose = 0)) - 1L
  correct    <- pred_class == y_val
  grid$val_acc[g] <- round(100 * mean(correct), 1)
  digit_acc[g, ]  <- round(100 * tapply(correct, meta_val$digit, mean), 1)
}

grid_digit <- cbind(grid, digit_acc)
dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(grid, "results/task5_grid.rds")
saveRDS(grid_digit, "results/task5_grid_digit.rds")
grid_digit


#sensitivity
range(grid$val_acc)                    
diff(range(grid$val_acc))              # spread across all 9 settings

tapply(grid$val_acc, grid$lr, mean)           # average by learning rate
tapply(grid$val_acc, grid$filters, mean)      # average by number of filters


#per-digit validation accuracy for the best model
best <- which.max(grid$val_acc)
grid[best, ]                                        

pred_best  <- max.col(models[[best]] |> predict(x_val, verbose = 0)) - 1L
acc_digit_best <- tapply(pred_best == y_val, meta[val_rows, ]$digit, mean)
round(100 * acc_digit_best, 1)
saveRDS(acc_digit_best, "results/task5_best_by_digit.rds")
```

Hyperparameter optimisation of the CNN was done with a grid search, which tries every combination of a fixed set of values. Results can depend strongly on a few hyperparameters, which is why tuning is worth checking [@probst2019]; other search methods exist [@bischl2023], but a small grid was enough for this brief. Optimisation was conducted by varying three values of the learning rate as well as three values of the number of filters while keeping all other hyperparameters constant. The learning rate controls how fast the model can learn and process before updating the weights while the number of filters sets how many patterns each convolution layer can pick up [@goodfellow2016]. The number of filters was set to 16, 32 and 64 and the learning rate to 0.0003, 0.001 and 0.003, which gives 9 combinations. The baseline CNN from Section 3 used the Adam optimiser with its default learning rate of 0.001 and had 32 filters in the first convolution layer and 64 in the second. The sensitivity to the hyperparameters was measured using the overall validation accuracy and the per-digit validation accuracy as in task 2.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-hyper
#| tbl-cap: "Overall validation accuracy (%) on session 4 for each combination of learning rate and number of filters, with row and column means. The baseline CNN uses a learning rate of 0.0010 and 32 filters."
grid <- readRDS("results/task5_grid.rds")

m <- tapply(grid$val_acc, list(grid$lr, grid$filters), mean)   # rows = learning rate, columns = filters
m <- rbind(m, Mean = colMeans(m))                               # average over learning rates
m <- cbind(m, Mean = rowMeans(m))                               # average over filter sizes (corner = overall mean)

rownames(m)[1:3] <- sprintf("%.4f", as.numeric(rownames(m)[1:3])) 
colnames(m)[1:3] <- paste(colnames(m)[1:3], "filters")

knitr::kable(m, digits = 1, align = "cccc")
```

```{r}
#| label: hyper-numbers
#| include: false
# Numbers for the hyperparameter text (all from the grid results)
hb <- which.max(grid$val_acc); hw <- which.min(grid$val_acc)
lr_best  <- sprintf("%.4f", grid$lr[hb]);  lr_worst <- sprintf("%.4f", grid$lr[hw])
best_base_txt <- if (is_base[hb]) " (the baseline configuration)" else ""
spread_pts <- diff(range(grid$val_acc))
lr_means <- tapply(grid$val_acc, grid$lr, mean)          # 0.0003, 0.001, 0.003
fl_means <- tapply(grid$val_acc, grid$filters, mean)     # 16, 32, 64
lr_rng <- diff(range(lr_means)); fl_rng <- diff(range(fl_means))
lr_trend_txt <- if (all(diff(lr_means) < 0)) "Accuracy fell as the learning rate rose." else
  if (all(diff(lr_means) > 0)) "Accuracy rose as the learning rate rose." else
  "Accuracy did not change steadily with the learning rate."
fl_trend_txt <- if (which.max(fl_means) == 2)
  "Accuracy was highest at 32 filters and lower with fewer and with more filters." else
  sprintf("Accuracy was highest at %s filters.", names(fl_means)[which.max(fl_means)])
sens_txt <- if (abs(lr_rng - fl_rng) < 0.5)
  sprintf("The averages differ by %s points across learning rates and %s points across numbers of filters, so neither hyperparameter is clearly more influential.", f1(lr_rng), f1(fl_rng)) else
  sprintf("The averages differ by %s points across learning rates and %s points across numbers of filters, which suggests that accuracy is more sensitive to %s.",
          f1(lr_rng), f1(fl_rng), if (lr_rng > fl_rng) "the learning rate" else "the number of filters")
gd_means <- colMeans(readRDS("results/task5_grid_digit.rds")[, paste0("Digit_", 0:4)])
dig_lo <- which.min(gd_means) - 1L; dig_hi <- which.max(gd_means) - 1L
# Extra numbers for the Section 6 text
ov_mean <- mean(grid$val_acc); ov_sd <- sd(grid$val_acc)
n_val_img <- length(y_val)
se_pp <- 100 * sqrt(ov_mean / 100 * (1 - ov_mean / 100) / n_val_img)     # binomial SE if images were independent
far_idx <- which(ov_mean - grid$val_acc > 3)
standout_txt <- if (length(far_idx) == 1)
  sprintf("Only the combination of a learning rate of %s with %s filters stands out, as the one setting more than 3 points below the mean.",
          sprintf("%.4f", grid$lr[far_idx]), grid$filters[far_idx]) else
  if (length(far_idx) == 0) "No setting stands out: none is more than 3 points below the mean." else
  sprintf("%d settings are more than 3 points below the mean.", length(far_idx))
sens_short <- if (abs(lr_rng - fl_rng) < 0.5) "so neither hyperparameter clearly dominates" else
  sprintf("so accuracy was more sensitive to %s", if (lr_rng > fl_rng) "the learning rate" else "the number of filters")
gd9 <- as.matrix(readRDS("results/task5_grid_digit.rds")[, paste0("Digit_", 0:4)])
fr_set <- friedman.test(gd9)                                  # settings as blocks, digits as treatments
w_set  <- unname(fr_set$statistic) / (nrow(gd9) * (ncol(gd9) - 1))
d_ord  <- order(gd_means, decreasing = TRUE) - 1L             # digits from best to worst
ord_cons <- if (fr_set$p.value < 0.05) "consistent" else "not consistent"
stable_txt <- if (fr_set$p.value < 0.05) "a stable ordering and not independent replication" else "no stable ordering"
```

Overall validation accuracy ranged from `r f1(min(grid$val_acc))`% to `r f1(max(grid$val_acc))`% across the nine settings (mean `r f1(ov_mean)`%, SD `r f1(ov_sd)`; @tbl-hyper). The best setting was a learning rate of `r lr_best` with `r grid$filters[hb]` filters at `r f1(grid$val_acc[hb])`%`r best_base_txt`, and the worst was a learning rate of `r lr_worst` with `r grid$filters[hw]` filters at `r f1(grid$val_acc[hw])`%, a spread of `r f1(spread_pts)` percentage points. Averaged over the other hyperparameter, validation accuracy was `r f1(lr_means[1])`%, `r f1(lr_means[2])`% and `r f1(lr_means[3])`% for learning rates of 0.0003, 0.001 and 0.003, and `r f1(fl_means[1])`%, `r f1(fl_means[2])`% and `r f1(fl_means[3])`% for 16, 32 and 64 filters. The ranges of these averages are `r f1(lr_rng)` and `r f1(fl_rng)` percentage points, `r sens_short`. With `r sp(n_val_img)` validation images the binomial standard error of an accuracy near `r f1(ov_mean)`% is about `r f1(se_pp)` percentage points, and the images are clustered by writer, so the true uncertainty is larger and differences of one or two points between settings should not be interpreted. Each setting was trained once with the same seed. The size of the gain from tuning differs between hyperparameters and between data sets, which is why tuning effort is usually focused on the few that matter most [@probst2019]. `r standout_txt`

```{r}
#| label: tbl-hyper-digit
#| tbl-cap: "Validation accuracy (%) on session 4, overall and by digit, for each combination of learning rate and number of filters. The last row is the mean across the nine settings."
gd   <- readRDS("results/task5_grid_digit.rds")
cols <- c("val_acc", paste0("Digit_", 0:4))

tab <- data.frame(`Learning rate` = sprintf("%.4f", gd$lr),
                  Filters = as.character(gd$filters),
                  gd[, cols], check.names = FALSE)

avg <- data.frame(`Learning rate` = "Mean", Filters = "all",
                  t(colMeans(gd[, cols])), check.names = FALSE)

tab <- rbind(tab, avg)
names(tab)[3:8] <- c("Overall", paste("Digit", 0:4))

knitr::kable(tab, digits = 1, align = rep("c", 8), row.names = FALSE)
```

In @tbl-hyper-digit, the mean validation accuracy over the nine settings was highest for digit `r d_ord[1]` (`r f1(gd_means[d_ord[1] + 1])`%) and digit `r d_ord[2]` (`r f1(gd_means[d_ord[2] + 1])`%) and lowest for digit `r d_ord[5]` (`r f1(gd_means[d_ord[5] + 1])`%) and digit `r d_ord[4]` (`r f1(gd_means[d_ord[4] + 1])`%). The order of the digits was `r ord_cons` across settings (Friedman chi-squared = `r f2(unname(fr_set$statistic), 1)` on `r unname(fr_set$parameter)` df, p `r fp(fr_set$p.value)`; Kendall's W = `r f2(w_set)`; settings as blocks). The nine models share the same data, so this shows `r stable_txt`.

# Comparison and discussion {#sec-compare}

```{r}
#| label: compare-stats
#| include: false
# Numbers for the comparison (all from objects created in earlier chunks)
gd7 <- readRDS("results/task5_grid_digit.rds")
gm  <- as.matrix(gd7[, paste0("Digit_", 0:4)])        # 9 settings x 5 digits, validation accuracy (%)
fr_grid <- friedman.test(gm)                          # settings as blocks, digits as treatments
w_grid  <- unname(fr_grid$statistic) / (nrow(gm) * (ncol(gm) - 1))
val9 <- colMeans(gm)
rk <- cbind(CNN_test = rank(-digit_stats$Accuracy), CNN_val9 = rank(-val9), Siamese = rank(-by_digit$Bal_acc))
rownames(rk) <- 0:4
mean_rk <- rowMeans(rk)
top_dg  <- names(which.min(mean_rk))
rk_span <- apply(rk, 1, function(v) max(v) - min(v))
move_dg <- names(which.max(rk_span))
order_desc <- function(v) join_and((0:4)[order(v, decreasing = TRUE)])
hi_s <- which.max(by_digit$Bal_acc) - 1L; lo_s <- which.min(by_digit$Bal_acc) - 1L
gap_cnn  <- 100 * (train_acc - test_acc)
drop_tmr <- 100 * (ss$Rate[1] - ss$Rate[2])
inside_txt <- if (val_acc_last >= boot_all[1] && val_acc_last <= boot_all[2]) "inside" else "outside"
se_val <- 100 * sqrt(mean(grid$val_acc) / 100 * (1 - mean(grid$val_acc) / 100) / length(y_val))
```

## What the two models measure

The CNN does identification: given one image it picks one of 20 known writers, so chance is 5%. The Siamese network does verification: given two images it decides whether one writer wrote both, so chance is 50%, and the test writers were never seen in training [@chicco2021]. The results in @tbl-compare-models therefore answer different questions and should not be ranked against each other. The CNN named the right writer for `r pc(test_acc)` of the session 5 images, about `r round(test_acc / 0.05)` times chance, and the Siamese network reached a balanced accuracy of `r f3(bal_hat)` with an AUC of `r f3(auc_hat)`. Choosing between two outcomes is easier than choosing among 20, so the higher Siamese score does not mean that it recognises writers better. The uncertainty also differs. The CNN interval comes from a cluster bootstrap that resamples writer-digit groups, which respects the dependence between near-copy images [@saravanan2020]. The Siamese intervals resample pairs that share images, so they are too narrow and are best read as a lower bound. The cluster bootstrap itself can be conservative when the data are closer to independent than assumed [@saravanan2020], so the CNN interval errs on the side of being too wide, which is the safer mistake here.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-compare-models
#| tbl-cap: "Summary of the two models on their held-out data. CP: exact Clopper-Pearson interval."
cmp_models <- data.frame(
  Item = c("Question", "Held-out data", "Chance level", "Main result"),
  CNN = c("Which of the 20 writers wrote this image?",
          sprintf("Session 5, known writers (%s images)", sp(n_test)),
          "0.05",
          sprintf("Accuracy %.3f (CP %.3f to %.3f; cluster bootstrap %.3f to %.3f)", test_acc, cp_all[1], cp_all[2], boot_all[1], boot_all[2])),
  Siamese = c("Did one writer write both images?",
              sprintf("Writers 18 to 20, unseen (%s pairs)", sp(n_pairs)),
              "0.50",
              sprintf("Balanced accuracy %.3f (%.3f to %.3f); AUC %.3f (%.3f to %.3f)", bal_hat, bal_ci[1], bal_ci[2], auc_hat, auc_ci[1], auc_ci[2])))
knitr::kable(cmp_models, row.names = FALSE, col.names = c("", "CNN (identification)", "Siamese network (verification)"))
```

## Which digits carry more writer information

```{r}
#| label: tbl-compare-digit
#| tbl-cap: "Writer information by digit. CNN test accuracy (%) with 95% cluster-bootstrap interval; mean CNN validation accuracy (%) over the nine tuning settings; Siamese balanced accuracy on test pairs with 95% bootstrap interval; and the Task 1 ratio of across-session to within-session pixel distance."
cmp <- data.frame(
  Digit = 0:4,
  cnn_test = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f to %.1f)", 100 * digit_stats$Accuracy, 100 * digit_stats$Boot_low, 100 * digit_stats$Boot_high),
  cnn_val9 = sprintf("%.1f", val9),
  siam     = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f to %.3f)", by_digit$Bal_acc, by_digit$CI_low, by_digit$CI_high),
  ratio    = sprintf("%.2f", rd$Ratio))
knitr::kable(cmp, row.names = FALSE, align = "ccccc",
             col.names = c("Digit", "CNN test accuracy", "CNN validation, mean of 9 settings",
                           "Siamese balanced accuracy", "Across / within distance"))
```

In Task 1 we expected digits 0 and 1, which vary most in shape (@sec-task1), to carry the most writer information. `r ifelse(top_dg %in% c("0", "1"), "The rankings broadly support this", "The rankings do not clearly support this")`: digit `r top_dg` ranked best on average, while digits 0 and 1 had mean ranks of `r f2(mean_rk[["0"]])` and `r f2(mean_rk[["1"]])`. @tbl-compare-digit puts the digit results side by side. From highest to lowest, the CNN test accuracy ranks the digits `r order_desc(digit_stats$Accuracy)`, the mean validation accuracy over the nine tuning settings ranks them `r order_desc(val9)`, and the Siamese balanced accuracy ranks them `r order_desc(by_digit$Bal_acc)`. After averaging the three ranks, digit `r top_dg` comes out best (mean rank `r f2(mean_rk[top_dg])`), and digit `r move_dg` is the least stable, moving over `r rk_span[move_dg]` places between the rankings. For the Siamese network, digit `r hi_s` scored highest (`r f3(by_digit$Bal_acc[hi_s + 1])`) and digit `r lo_s` lowest (`r f3(by_digit$Bal_acc[lo_s + 1])`), although the pairs are not independent, so these intervals are optimistic (@fig-t3-digit).

The evidence that digits differ is weaker than the rankings suggest. For the CNN test accuracy, a Friedman test with writers as blocks gave chi-squared = `r f2(unname(fr2$statistic), 2)` on `r unname(fr2$parameter)` df, p `r fp(fr2$p.value)` (Kendall's W = `r f2(w2)`), and the bootstrap intervals overlap almost completely. Across the nine tuning settings the ordering of digits was more consistent (Friedman chi-squared = `r f2(unname(fr_grid$statistic), 1)` on `r unname(fr_grid$parameter)` df, p `r fp(fr_grid$p.value)`; W = `r f2(w_grid)`). However, those nine models share the same training and validation images, so this shows a stable ordering within one data set and not that it would reappear for new writers. The pixel distances of Task 1 did not predict the ranking either: digit `r rd$Digit[hi_r]` had the largest across-session to within-session ratio (`r f2(rd$Ratio[hi_r])`), yet it ranked `r ord_word[rk[as.character(rd$Digit[hi_r]), "CNN_test"]]` for CNN test accuracy and `r ord_word[rk[as.character(rd$Digit[hi_r]), "Siamese"]]` for the Siamese network. Taken together, digit `r top_dg` carried the most writer information in this data set, every digit carried far more than chance, and the differences between digits are small next to the differences between writers (@fig-t2-writer).

## How a change of session affects performance

Task 1 showed that a change of session moves a writer's digit about `r pc(frac_session, 0)` of the way towards another writer's digit, and both models paid for it. The CNN fitted its training sessions to `r pc(train_acc)` and the randomly split validation images to `r pc(rand_val_acc)`, where near copies were in the training set. On the new sessions it reached `r pc(val_acc_last)` (session 4) and `r pc(test_acc)` (session 5), a drop of about `r round(gap_cnn)` points from training. The session 4 accuracy lies `r inside_txt` the session 5 bootstrap interval, so the two held-out sessions cannot be told apart. The validation loss rose from `r f2(val_loss_1)` to `r f2(val_loss_end)` while the training loss fell, which is the usual sign of overfitting [@goodfellow2016].

The Siamese network shows the same effect more precisely. All `r ss$n[1]` same-writer pairs from one session were accepted, against `r pc0(ss$Rate[2])` of the `r ss$n[2]` same-writer pairs from different sessions (Fisher exact p `r fp(p_same_writer_sessions)`; @tbl-t3-session). Different-writer pairs showed no clear session effect (`r pc0(ss$Rate[3])` against `r pc0(ss$Rate[4])`, p `r fp(p_diff_writer_sessions)`). A change of session therefore caused false rejections of the same writer and not false matches. The Fisher test treats pairs as independent, so its p-value is too small, but the gap is large. The drops (about `r round(gap_cnn)` points for the CNN and `r f1(drop_tmr)` points in the Siamese true match rate) cannot be compared directly because the tasks and writers differ. Their direction agrees with the evidence that testing on near copies of the training data overstates performance [@roberts2017; @saeb2017; @kapoor2023].

## Limitations and summary

The data are simulated, the CNN result rests on one held-out session, and the Siamese result rests on three writers. Each model was trained once with a fixed seed, so seed-to-seed variation was not measured. The nine tuning settings spanned `r f1(spread_pts)` percentage points, and with 5 000 validation images the binomial standard error of an accuracy near `r f1(mean(grid$val_acc))`% is about `r f1(se_val)` points before dependence is allowed for, so differences of one or two points between settings should not be interpreted. The two models were also not compared on the same footing. A fairer test would score both on the same pairs, for example by using the CNN's hidden layer as an embedding.

In summary, a CNN trained on sessions 1 to 3 identified the writer in `r pc(test_acc)` of the images from a new session, far above the 5% chance level but well below its training accuracy. A Siamese network separated same-writer from different-writer pairs of unseen writers with a balanced accuracy of `r f3(bal_hat)`. Digit `r top_dg` carried the most writer information, but the differences between digits were small. A change of session lowered performance in both models, mainly by making the same writer look like a different one.
